# Title 47
## Subpart J—Equipment Authorization Procedures
### Application Procedures for Equipment Authorizations
#### § 2.925 Identification of equipment.
The FCC Identifier assigned to any transmitter section shall be preceded by the term *TX FCC ID,* the FCC Identifier assigned to any receiver section shall be preceded by the term *RX FCC ID* and the identifier assigned to any remaining section(s) shall be preceded by the term *FCC ID.*
#### § 2.926 FCC identifier.
(a) A grant of certification will list the validated FCC Identifier consisting of the grantee code assigned by the FCC pursuant to paragraph (b) of this section, and the equipment product code assigned by the grantee pursuant to paragraph (c) of this section.
The FCC Identifier is uniquely assigned to the grantee and may not be placed on the equipment without authorization by the grantee.  Labeling of such equipment may include model or type numbers, but shall not include a purported FCC Identifier.

Its tasks include the development of technical standards for radio equipment. Testing for compliance with these standards is required for market approval of most devices that use radio technologies.

  Federal Communications Commission (FCC) 

 The  Federal Communications Commission (FCC)  , created by the Communications Act in 1934, is responsible for the proper development and operation of broadcasting services. It is also the licensing authority for communications equipment such as radios, televisions and computers. Certification is required for all electronic products manufactured and sold in the United States.

 The appropriate method for certifying equipment depends on the specific sections of FCC rules relevant to the particular radio operation. In the absence of a specified policy, intentional radiators (i.e., transmitters) require the certification process issued by an FCC-approved  Telecommunications Certification Body (TCB)  .

## FCC Part 15: Intentional Radiators (Equipment Certification)

Products that intentionally emit radio-frequency energy under FCC Part 15 (for example Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and other short-range wireless transmitters) must in almost all cases be certified before they can be marketed or imported into the United States. seltz.title: FCC ID, Grantee Code & TCB: equipment authorization
seltz.snippet:
An FCC ID is not a product number the manufacturer invents. It is two elements in a fixed order, a Grantee Code the FCC assigns once per company and a product code of 14 characters at most, and it only becomes valid when a TCB publishes a grant of certification. This page reads the sections of 47 CFR Part 2 Subpart J and Part 15 that build that identifier, the role of the TCB, the label, modular approval and permissive changes, with the changes made by the 2023 to 2026 Covered List and TCB integrity orders.

The rules live in 47 CFR Part 2 Subpart J. For the devices this page covers, Subpart J offers two procedures:

- **SDoC** (Supplier's Declaration of Conformity, 2.906): the responsible party makes the measurements and keeps the records. Nothing is filed with the FCC unless a sample or data is requested under 2.945.
- **Certification** (2.907): a grant "approved by the Commission or issued by a Telecommunication Certification Body (TCB)", based on the test data the applicant submits. It attaches to every unit marketed by the grantee that is identical to the sample tested, except for permissive changes under 2.1043.

The route is set by the rule part, not chosen freely, which is the US counterpart of the split discussed in self-declaration vs Notified Body. 2.906(c) lets any SDoC device be certified instead, and since FCC 22-84 equipment produced by an entity on the Covered List can only use Certification (2.906(d), 2.907(c)).

seltz.title: FCC Rules for Electronics Sellers: Listings Count as Marketing
seltz.snippet:
Sellers importing electronics from overseas suppliers usually think of FCC compliance as an import checkpoint. Clear customs and you are through.

The rule is broader than that. Under 47 CFR 2.803, marketing includes advertising, which means the product listing itself is a marketing act. Publishing a listing for an unauthorised radio frequency device is a violation before a single unit ships.

There is no FCC rule aimed at online marketplaces as such. The exposure comes from the definition of marketing, which was written wide enough to cover the listing.

## Key takeaways

- Marketing includes advertising for sale, which captures online listings.
- No radio frequency device may be marketed without a valid FCC equipment authorization.
- Certification and Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity are two different procedures.
- FCC IDs exist only for certified equipment. SDoC devices do not have one.
- Intentional radiators such as Wi-Fi and Bluetooth generally require Certification.
- The catch-all forfeiture limit is $25,132 per violation with a $188,491 cap.

## What the rule says

Section 2.803(a) defines marketing as “sale or lease, or offering for sale or lease, including advertising for sale or lease, or importation, shipment, or distribution for the purpose of selling or leasing or offering for sale or lease.”

Section 2.803(b) sets the prohibition: “No person may market a radio frequency device unless the radio frequency device is authorized pursuant to a valid FCC equipment authorization”.

The underlying statute at 47 U.S.C. 302(b) is similarly broad: “No person shall manufacture, import, sell, offer for sale, or ship device or home electronic equipment and systems, or use devices, which fail to comply with regulations promulgated pursuant to this section.”

Note “offering for sale” appears in both. A live listing with no stock in the country is still an offer.

## FCC ID Requirements – United States

An FCC ID is a unique equipment authorization identifier defined by the grantee for radio frequency devices subject to the Certification procedure under U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) rules. It links a certified device to its official authorization record in the FCC Equipment Authorization System.

## Key Takeaways

- An FCC ID is issued only under the Certification procedure.

- It confirms that a Grant of Equipment Authorization has been issued.

- Certification is reviewed by an FCC-recognized Telecommunications Certification Body (TCB).

- The certified configuration is recorded in the public FCC database.

- Devices authorized solely under the Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity (SDoC) procedure do not receive an FCC ID.

- Product modifications may require permissive change filing or a new FCC ID.

## When an FCC ID Is Required

Devices subject to the Certification procedure under 47 CFR Part 2 require an FCC ID prior to marketing or importation.

This typically includes:

- Intentional radiators operating under Part 15 (e.g., Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, UWB, NFC)

- Devices operating under licensed service rule parts (e.g., Parts 22, 24, 27, 90, and 95)

- Transmitters integrated into composite or multi-radio devices

- Host devices incorporating certified radio modules where additional authorization is required

Where a device combines transmitting and non-transmitting functions, the transmitting portion is subject to Certification and must be covered by an FCC ID.
